body.text: Lorna Iseu always wanted a big family.
As a mother of five, she got her wish, but she wouldn't necessarily encourage others to do the same.
"I've now realised having a big family isn't cheap," she said.
"I'd encourage couples to have at least two or three children. For me, five is quite stressful."
Papua New Guinea's prime minister, James Marape, may well agree.
His government has announced plans to introduce a new national family planning policy to curb the country's high birth rate.

Under the proposed policy outlined in a press release, families would be encouraged to have no more than three children, in a move that draws comparisons with China's now-abandoned one-child policy, which remained in place until 2015.
While still at the proposal stage, PNG's policy aims to prevent unplanned pregnancies, ease pressure on government services and household budgets, and slow the country's population growth.
Official statistics put PNG's population at about 10.18 million, and it's growing by more than 180,000 people annually.
But economists question the reliability of the country's census data, suggesting the actual population could be closer to 12 million.
Teenage pregnancies and high rural birth rates are among the factors believed to be contributing to the country's population surge.
Health experts also say limited access to health care and contraception is forcing many women to have more children than they would otherwise choose to have.
Hidden figures
Ms Iseu lives in the country's capital, Port Moresby.
Her husband works as a security guard, while she stays home to look after her three youngest children.
Her two eldest attend school.
"My children can't even sit properly in the classroom. Some sit on desks, many are on the floor; it's so overcrowded," she said.
Margaret Ropa, also a mother of five from Port Moresby, agrees, saying the sheer number of children in the public school system has forced her to send her children to private school.
"You have 85 kids in a classroom,"
A 2025 national reform road map, titled Reset@50, which outlines the government's priorities for the next 20 years, notes PNG's fertility rate at 3.6 children per woman.
The document reports an adolescent birth rate of 64.9 births per 1,000 girls and women aged 15 to 19, well above the global average of about 38 per 1,000, according to World Bank data.
Meanwhile, only 25 per cent of women of reproductive age used modern contraceptive methods.
A fertility rate of 3.6 in a country of 10 million equates to roughly 250,000 to 300,000 births a year.
Kingtau Mambon, an economics lecturer at the University of Papua New Guinea, told the ABC that PNG's annual number of births was likely at the top end of that range.
"I've talked to doctors, and they say the birth rate is around 300,000 per year," he said.
Mr Mambon believes the National Statistical Office's population figure of 10.18 million is likely low, saying the real figure could be as high as 12 million.
He said the most recent census, in 2024, may not be fully accurate because it included only six questions and was affected by logistical and administrative breakdowns.
He said he had to go looking for census officers to take the survey.
"I was actually running after the people who brought the questionnaires," he said.
"They should have been looking for me."
The ABC contacted the PNG government for comment on the country's population, the census and the proposed policy.

Mr Mambon said he spoke to many people in central Port Moresby who did not complete the census, and he believed the same was true in rural areas, where he sees most of the population growth occurring.
He said customs around land ownership were one reason families were so large.
"The thing with PNG is, men own the land, and to defend the land you need a lot of people," he said.
"So men have to pursue the interests of protecting the land and tribal heritage.
"They have to have more kids."
Mr Mambon said stigma around contraception in rural areas was also pushing fertility rates higher.
"Many of the health facilities are being run by NGOs of faith-based organisations," he said.
"From the faith-based point of view, some don't want to give out contraceptives."
A holistic approach
Ms Ropa said she believed the government was doing the right thing with its policy proposal, but was sceptical about how it would be taken up, particularly in villages and rural areas.

Anjelique Giranah, country director of Marie Stopes PNG, an NGO providing family planning and reproductive health services, said encouraging people to have fewer children wouldn't work unless the government empowered women to have a bigger say in family sizes.
She said limited access to health care and contraception, as well as expectations from family and spouses, meant women were having more children than they wanted.
"National research confirms many women who want to delay or avoid having children are not able to access the contraception they need," she said.
"For us, meaningful choice means a woman can access reliable information and a range of contraceptive options and at the same time make that voluntary decision without pressure or coercion."
